extracted.intended_audience: UK government departments, policy teams and civil servants conducting public consultations
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for designing and running public consultations in the UK government context, covering clarity, purpose, targeting, timing, publication and response practices. Intended to ensure consultations are effective, proportionate and accountable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consultations should be clear and concise
rubrics_metrics.description: Use plain English and avoid acronyms. Be clear what questions you are asking and limit the number of questions to those that are necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make consultations easy to understand and easy to answer. Avoid lengthy documents when possible and consider merging consultations on related topics. Limit unnecessary questions and use accessible language to increase response quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consultations should have a purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not consult for the sake of it. Consult about policies or implementation plans when development is at a formative stage and take consultation responses into account when taking policy forward.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask departmental lawyers whether you have a legal duty to consult. Do not ask questions about issues on which you already have a final view. Use responses to inform policy decisions rather than merely as a box-ticking exercise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consultations should be informative
rubrics_metrics.description: Give enough information to ensure that those consulted understand the issues and can give informed responses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include validated impact assessments of the costs and benefits of the options being considered when possible; this may be required where proposals affect business or the voluntary sector. Provide sufficient background and evidence so consultees can evaluate options.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consultations are only part of a process of engagement
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider whether informal iterative consultation is appropriate; consultation is not just about formal documents and responses but is an ongoing process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use new digital tools and open, collaborative approaches where appropriate. Consider informal, iterative engagement in addition to formal written consultations to develop policy with stakeholders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consultations should last for a proportionate amount of time
rubrics_metrics.description: Judge the length of the consultation on the basis of legal advice and the nature and impact of the proposal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid consulting for too long (which delays policy development) and avoid consulting too quickly (which reduces quality of responses). Take legal advice where timing has statutory implications and balance thoroughness with timeliness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consultations should be targeted
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider the full range of people, businesses and voluntary bodies affected by the policy, and whether representative groups exist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Target specific groups where appropriate, ensure they are aware of the consultation and can access it. Consider how to tailor consultation methods to the needs and preferences of particular groups (e.g., older people, younger people, people with disabilities) who may not respond to traditional methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consultations should take account of the groups being consulted
rubrics_metrics.description: Consult stakeholders in a way that suits them; different groups may need different approaches or timeframes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognise that, for example, charities may need more time to respond than businesses. When consultation spans holiday periods, consider mitigating actions such as prior discussion with key interested parties or extending the consultation deadline beyond the holiday period.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consultations should be agreed before publication
rubrics_metrics.description: Seek collective agreement before publishing a written consultation, particularly when consulting on new policy proposals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure consultations are agreed internally before launch. Consultations should be published on gov.uk so they are accessible and discoverable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consultation should facilitate scrutiny
rubrics_metrics.description: Publish any response on the same page on gov.uk as the original consultation and make it clear when the government has responded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain the responses received from consultees and how these have informed the policy. State how many responses have been received to enable public scrutiny of engagement and outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government responses to consultations should be published in a timely fashion
rubrics_metrics.description: Publish responses within 12 weeks of the consultation or provide an explanation why this is not possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where consultation concerns a statutory instrument, publish responses before or at the same time as the instrument is laid except in very exceptional circumstances (and even then publish responses as soon as possible). Allow appropriate time between closing the consultation and implementing policy or legislation to reflect findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consultation exercises should not generally be launched during local or national election periods
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid launching consultations during election periods unless exceptional circumstances make it absolutely essential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a consultation is essential during an election period (e.g., safeguarding public health), seek advice from the Propriety and Ethics team in the Cabinet Office. Note that this guidance does not have legal force and remains subject to statutory and other legal requirements.
